current_activity: parachute drop west of Le Muy; no trooper lands on the assigned zones, battalions scattered from Trans to Lorgues
notes: Event date: 15 August 1944, about 0435 (Clarke and Smith, ch. 6, p. 101). Event definition: None of the combat team lands on its drop zones, centred two miles west of Le Muy; the 1st Battalion is scattered from Trans-en-Provence to Lorgues, much of the 2nd lands near La Motte, the 3rd far to the north-east; most of the 1st and 2nd Battalions reach their assembly areas after dawn (Clarke and Smith, ch. 6). Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH), and Wikipedia). Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 6, p. 101: "None of the troopers of the 517th Parachute regimental combat team landed on their assigned drop zones"; Wikipedia, 1st Airborne Task Force: "The U.S. 517th PRCT were assigned an area of narrow fields about two miles west of Le Muy". Location: Le Muy, Var (new place) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is Le Muy; the drop zone was about two miles west of it and the troopers were scattered over a wide area, so the precision is 10 km. Location support: Clarke and Smith place the drop zones two miles west of Le Muy. Commander: Colonel Rupert D. Graves (Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team).

current_activity: beats off the German attack from Vidauban at Les Arcs, then nearly surrounds the town by dusk
notes: Event date: 16 August 1944 (Clarke and Smith, ch. 7). Event definition: West of Le Muy the 517th meets the first organised German response at Les Arcs; it holds the hills north-east and east of the town, then attacks late in the day with its 3rd Battalion and by dusk has nearly surrounded Les Arcs; the Germans withdraw in the night (Clarke and Smith, ch. 7). Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH), and Wikipedia). Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 7, p. 118: "West of Le Muy, at Les Arcs, the 517th Parachute Infantry had begun to run into the first signs of an organized German response"; Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 7, p. 119: "Late in the day, reinforced by its 3d Battalion, the 517th Parachute Infantry launched an attack of its own, and by dusk had virtually surrounded Les Arcs"; Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team: "capturing Le Muy , Les Arcs , La Motte and Draguignan". Location: Les Arcs, Var (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Clarke and Smith and Wikipedia name Les Arcs. Commander: Colonel Rupert D. Graves (Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team).

current_activity: on the left of the task force, takes Saint-Cézaire after Fayence and Callian
notes: Event date: 22 August 1944 (Wikipedia). Event definition: In the task force advance east to the line Fayence-La Napoule, the combat team on the left takes Fayence and Callian by 21 August and Companies G and I take Saint-Cézaire on the 22nd (Wikipedia). Event support: one source family (Wikipedia). Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team: "The 517th RCT was assigned the left, the Special Service Force the center and the 509th/551st PIR the right"; "fell to Companies G and I on the 22nd". Location: Saint-Cézaire-sur-Siagne, Alpes-Maritimes (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Wikipedia names Saint-Cézaire. Commander: Colonel Rupert D. Graves (Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team).

current_activity: Maritime Alps: takes high ground near the Col de Braus; heavy fighting follows
notes: Event date: 5 September 1944 (Wikipedia). Event definition: Moving east of Nice, the combat team attacks the forts guarding the approach to Sospel; on 5 September Company D takes high ground near the Col de Braus and Companies G and H later capture the pass (Wikipedia). Event support: one source family (Wikipedia). Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team: "On 5 September, Company D succeeded in taking some high ground near Col de Braus". Location: Col de Braus, Alpes-Maritimes (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Wikipedia names the Col de Braus. Commander: Colonel Rupert D. Graves (Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team).

current_activity: patrol pushes into Sospel; the Germans withdraw after 51 days
notes: Event date: 29 September 1944 (Wikipedia). Event definition: Despite heavy artillery fire a patrol of Company F pushes into Sospel on 29 September and the Germans withdraw (Wikipedia). Event support: one source family (Wikipedia). Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team: "a patrol from Company F pushed into Sospel on 29 September". Location: Sospel, Alpes-Maritimes (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Wikipedia names Sospel. Commander: Colonel Rupert D. Graves (Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team).

current_activity: all elements quartered at Soissons under the XVIII Airborne Corps
notes: Event date: 10 December 1944 (Wikipedia). Event definition: The combat team entrains at Antibes on 6 December for Soissons and assignment to the XVIII Airborne Corps; all elements are at Soissons by 10 December (Wikipedia). Event support: one source family (Wikipedia). Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team: "All elements of the RCT were quartered in Soissons by 10 December". Location: Soissons, Aisne (new place) with a precision of 5 km. Location support: Wikipedia names Soissons. Commander: Colonel Rupert D. Graves (Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team). Context: Relationship: the 1st Airborne Task Force attachment was closed on 17 November 1944, the day the combat team left the Alpine campaign (inferred value; Wikipedia).

current_activity: 1st Battalion reaches Soy at twilight and is committed at once against the Soy-Hotton road
notes: Event date: 22 December 1944, twilight (Cole, ch. 16). Event definition: The long-awaited 1st Battalion arrives at Soy at twilight with a tank destroyer company and is committed at once by the 3rd Armored Division to reopen the road to Hotton (Cole, ch. 16); Wikipedia says the battalion went to the 3rd Armored sector near Soy on XVIII Airborne Corps orders. Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH), and Wikipedia). Cole, The Ardennes, ch. 16, p. 384: "Long awaited, the 1st Battalion of the 517th Parachute Infantry and a company from the 643d Tank Destroyer Battalion arrived in Soy at twilight"; Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team: "directed the 1st Battalion to the 3rd Armored Division sector near Soy, Belgium". Location: Soy, Luxembourg (Belgium) (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Cole and Wikipedia name Soy. Commander: Colonel Rupert D. Graves (Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team).

current_activity: 3rd Battalion retakes Manhay in a night assault after an eight-battalion concentration
notes: Event date: 27 December 1944, by 0400 (Cole, ch. 23). Event definition: Ridgway uses the fresh 3rd Battalion, just back from helping the 30th Division at La Gleize, for a night assault on Manhay; after midnight and a twenty-minute concentration it clears the village by 0400 on 27 December (Cole, ch. 23; Wikipedia). Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH), and Wikipedia). Cole, The Ardennes, ch. 23, p. 598: "General Ridgway decided to use the fresh 3d Battalion of the 517th Parachute Infantry"; Cole, The Ardennes, ch. 23, p. 598: "By 0400 on 27 December the paratroopers had cleared the village"; Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team: "General Ridgeway was ordered to retake Manhay at all costs". Location: Manhay, Luxembourg (Belgium) (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Cole and Wikipedia name Manhay. Commander: Colonel Rupert D. Graves (Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team). Context: Relationship: the 3rd Armored Division attachment of the 1st Battalion (from 22 December) is not closed here; this row is the 3rd Battalion under XVIII Airborne Corps orders.

current_activity: on the 82nd Airborne left, attacks south along the Salm; 2nd Battalion takes Trois-Ponts
notes: Event date: 3 January 1945 (MacDonald, ch. 2; Wikipedia). Event definition: Attached to the 82nd Airborne Division, the regiment jumps off with the VII Corps on 3 January as the division's left flank along the Salm; the 2nd Battalion takes Trois-Ponts (Wikipedia); it turns to take the Germans in flank on 7 January and holds a small bridgehead over the Salm on the 9th (MacDonald, ch. 2). Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH), and Wikipedia). MacDonald, The Last Offensive, ch. 2, p. 32: "Assisted by an attached separate regiment, the 517th Parachute Infantry, the airborne division jumped off along with the VII Corps on 3 January"; Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team: "On 3 January, the RCT, acting as the left flank of the 82nd, attacked south along the Salm River"; "the 2nd Battalion captured Trois-Ponts". Location: Trois-Ponts, Liège (new place) with a precision of 5 km. Location support: Wikipedia names Trois-Ponts. Commander: Colonel Rupert D. Graves (Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team). Context: Relationship: the 3rd Armored Division attachment of the 1st Battalion is closed the day before (inferred value).

current_activity: with the 106th Infantry Division, attacks south from the Ambleve near Stavelot towards Poteaux
notes: Event date: 13 January 1945, 0800 (Wikipedia; MacDonald, ch. 2). Event definition: Attached to the 106th Infantry Division, the combat team relieves the 112th Infantry at Stavelot on 12 January and attacks at 0800 on the 13th towards the line Spineux-Poteaux (Wikipedia); MacDonald puts the 106th Division in the Salm-Ambleve angle with the separate 517th. Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH), and Wikipedia). MacDonald, The Last Offensive, ch. 2, p. 45: "pressed forward in the angle itself with the separate 517th Parachute Infantry"; Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team: "relieve the 112th Infantry at Stavelot"; "A new attack was launched at 0800 on 13 January". Location: Stavelot, Liège (new place) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is Stavelot, the start; the attack went about 8 miles south, so the precision is 10 km. Location support: Wikipedia names Stavelot. Commander: Colonel Rupert D. Graves (Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team). Context: Relationship: the 82nd Airborne Division attachment is closed the day before (inferred value).

current_activity: with the 78th Infantry Division, attacks south from Bergstein towards the Schmidt-Nideggen ridge
notes: Event date: 5 February 1945 (Wikipedia). Event definition: Attached to the 78th Infantry Division on 3 February, the combat team closes at Kleinhau by 0600 on 5 February and attacks south from Bergstein that night towards the Schmidt-Nideggen ridge (Wikipedia). Event support: one source family (Wikipedia). Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team: "on 3 February, the RCT received orders attaching it to the 78th Infantry Division at Simmerath"; "all units had closed at Kleinhau". Location: Kleinhau, North Rhine-Westphalia (new place) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is Kleinhau, the assembly area; the attack went south from Bergstein, about 2 km away. Location support: Wikipedia names Kleinhau and Bergstein. Commander: Colonel Rupert D. Graves (Wikipedia, 517th Parachute Regimental Combat Team). Context: Relationship: the 106th Infantry Division attachment is closed on 2 February (inferred value).
